course_name: Algorithms and Data Structures. Part 1. Basics of Algorithmization

course_profile.one_sentence_summary: A foundational course on algorithmic logic, problem-solving methods, and basic linear data structures for software engineering students.
course_profile.short_summary: This course introduces first-year software engineering students to the core concepts of algorithmization. It covers linear, branching, and cyclic algorithm design, alongside mathematical foundations like combinatorics and recursion. Students learn fundamental search and sorting algorithms, approximate calculations, and basic linear data structures (arrays, stacks, queues, linked lists) with practical implementation using flowcharts and pseudocode.

theoretical_understanding: Understand the properties of algorithms and standard approaches to evaluating their correctness.
Understand Big-O notation and evaluate the time complexity of iterative and search algorithms.
Comprehend the fundamental theories behind sorting, searching, recursion, and basic combinatorial operations.
practical_implementation: Create rigorous flowcharts using tools like MS Visio and Draw.io according to standard specifications.
Write pseudocode and implement algorithms for linear sequence processing, branching, and cyclic tasks.
Implement classic searching (binary, interpolation) and sorting (elementary, quicksort) algorithms.
Implement and manipulate arrays, stacks, queues, and linked lists.
analysis_validation: Analyze absolute and relative errors in approximate calculations.
Test algorithms for correctness and process execution results.
architecture_design: Design modular solutions by utilizing auxiliary (helper) algorithms.
Design physical memory layouts and operations for linked data structures.
research_and_prototyping: Compare the efficiency and complexity tradeoffs between iterative and recursive algorithmic solutions.

implementation_tasks: Designing linear, branching, and cyclic algorithms.
Building and interacting with linear data structures (linked lists).
engineering_practices: Formal problem definition and model building

curricular_relations.reason: Understanding how to construct an algorithm is required before analyzing its time complexity.
Basic data structures like arrays and lists are the foundations upon which searching and sorting algorithms operate.
Knowledge of discrete mathematics supports the design of algorithms involving combinatorics and discrete subsets.
Prior basic programming knowledge is required to formalize and execute the designed algorithmic logic.

what_student_can_understand: How to mathematically and logically evaluate the efficiency and constraints of software algorithms.
The underlying mechanics and memory distribution of standard data structures like arrays, stacks, queues, and lists.
what_student_can_build: Standard flowcharts and structured pseudocode to represent complex business logic.
Linear data structures from scratch using primitive arrays or pointers.
what_student_can_apply: Core problem-solving frameworks to translate a written problem into a formal algorithmic sequence.
Basic mathematical and bitwise operations to optimize computational processes.

evidence.claim: The course evaluates students based on flowcharts, pseudocode, code correctness, and testing.
